prompt: Match each modifier to the widest set of classes that may use a member declared with it.
hint: The table in section 02.

pairs.right: Every class in the same package

right_distractors: Only the `main` method of the class

prompt: `Main`, outside `lib`, read `s.code`, where `code` is declared with no modifier. What did `javac` say?
hint: No modifier is not the same as public.

choices.text: Nothing: a field with no modifier is public by default
choices.why: That is the belief the error corrects; with no modifier, only the package sees it.

choices.text: That `code` is not public in `Shelf` and cannot be accessed from outside the package
choices.why: Right: no modifier means package-private.

choices.text: That `code` has private access in `Shelf`
choices.why: That message was for `count`, which is declared `private`.

choices.text: That `code` has protected access in `Shelf`
choices.why: That message was for `capacity`.

prompt: `lib/Inside.java`, in the same package as `Shelf`, read `s.code`, `s.capacity` and `s.count`. Which failed?
hint: One modifier excludes even the neighbours.

choices.text: `s.count` alone
choices.why: Right: private means this class and nothing else, not even a class in the same package.

choices.text: `s.capacity` and `s.count`
choices.why: `protected` includes the package, so `capacity` passed.

choices.text: None of them: inside the package every member is visible
choices.why: `count` failed with `count has private access in Shelf`.

choices.text: All three, because `Inside` is a different class
choices.why: Being a different class matters only for `private`; the package is shared.

prompt: `Shelf` has a private field `count` and a public method `count()`. What may `Main`, in another package, do with the count?
hint: A field and a method can share a name.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: `s.count()` compiled and printed 2.

choices.text: Read it and change it, through the field
choices.why: The field is private; that is the third error in section 02.

choices.text: Read it, through `count()`
choices.why: Right: the method is public and only returns the value.

prompt: A member declared with no modifier at all is called ___-private.
hint: Who may use it?

prompt: Why does the section say secrecy is the wrong reason to make a field private?
hint: Who can read the source?

choices.text: Because private fields are copied into every class file anyway
choices.why: A private field is in its own class's file only; that is not the argument.

choices.text: Anyone with the source sees the name; the point is that nobody else changes it
choices.why: Right: private protects a promise about the data, not the data's existence.

choices.text: Because `javap -p` prints private fields and so reveals them
choices.why: `javap -p` does print them, but the argument is about change, not about seeing.

prompt: In `OpenMain`, after `loan.renewals = 7;`, `renew()` returned `true`. What did the program print for the count right after?
hint: The check compares with 2 and nothing else.

prompt: `renew()` refuses when `renewals == 2`. After the count was set to 7 from outside, why does it never refuse again?
hint: Follow the count: 7, 8, 9...

choices.text: The assignment reset the method, which now starts from zero
choices.why: Methods hold no state of their own; the count is the field, and it is at 8.

choices.text: The count passed 2 without ever equalling it, and the check is `==`
choices.why: Right: from 7 it only grows, so `renewals == 2` is never true again.

choices.text: An `int` field wraps round after 2 when it is set from another class
choices.why: Nothing wraps; 7 became 8, as printed.

choices.text: `OpenLoan` is package-private, so its methods are skipped from outside
choices.why: `renew()` ran and returned `true`; package-private hides nothing in the same directory.

prompt: With `private int renewals;`, where can the code that changes the count be?
hint: `Cheat` tried from outside.

choices.text: Anywhere in the same package
choices.why: That would be package-private; private excludes the package.

choices.text: In `Loan` and in any class that calls `renewals()`
choices.why: `renewals()` only reads the count; nothing outside `Loan` can write it.

choices.text: In code written inside `Loan` itself
choices.why: Right: so to check the rule you read one class.

prompt: A teammate argues: "Make every field public now; we can make them private later if it matters." What does the section answer?
hint: Which mistake is cheap to fix later?

choices.text: Public fields are slower, so it matters at once
choices.why: Speed is not the section's argument, and access does not change it.

choices.text: Too loose is hard to tighten later, because other code comes to depend on it; too strict costs one compile error
choices.why: Right: start from private and open what a real use needs.

choices.text: Agreed, since the compiler will list every place to fix when you change it
choices.why: It will, and some of those places may be code you do not own and cannot change.

prompt: A file `Catalogue.java` declares `public class Catalogue` and `public class Entry`. What happens?
hint: Where would the compiler look for `Entry`?

choices.text: It compiles, and `Entry` is usable only inside the file
choices.why: It does not compile; and non-public would mean the package, not the file.

choices.text: It compiles into one class file holding both classes
choices.why: There is always one `.class` per class, and here there is an error first.

choices.text: An error: `Entry` is public and should be in `Entry.java`
choices.why: Right: a public class must be in a file named after it.

prompt: With `Entry` made non-public, `javac Catalogue.java` succeeded. How many `.class` files did it write?
hint: `ls` listed them.

prompt: `Entry` without `public` sits in `Catalogue.java`. Which classes may use it?
hint: It is package-private now.

choices.text: Only `Catalogue`, because it is in `Catalogue`'s file
choices.why: Access follows the package, not the file.

choices.text: Any class in the same package, in any of its files
choices.why: Right: no modifier means package-private, whichever file it is in.

choices.text: Any class anywhere, since `Catalogue` is public
choices.why: A public class does not make its neighbours public.

prompt: Why must a public class live in a file named after it?
hint: Think about another class, somewhere else, that mentions `Entry`.

choices.text: So that the JVM can load `.java` files directly
choices.why: The JVM loads only class files; the rule is for the compiler.

choices.text: Because a file name is the class's identity at run time
choices.why: At run time the class file carries the name; the source file's name is gone.

choices.text: So the compiler can find its source by its name
choices.why: Right: a reference to `Entry` from anywhere sends the compiler to `Entry.java`.

prompt: Order the four access levels from the most closed to the most open.
hint: Each one reaches everything the one before it reaches.

prompt: A class `Member` has a field `fines` that must never go below zero. Which design lets one class keep that promise?
hint: Which code can change the field in each design?

choices.text: `public double fines;` and a comment saying it must not be negative
choices.why: A comment binds nobody; any class can assign `-5`.

choices.text: `private double fines;`, changed only by methods that check it
choices.why: Right: then every change passes through code in `Member`, like `renew()` in `Loan`.

choices.text: `protected double fines;`, so that only subclasses change it
choices.why: Protected still includes the whole package, and any subclass anywhere.

choices.text: `double fines;` with no modifier, so that other packages cannot reach it
choices.why: Every class in the package can still assign it, which is most of the program.

prompt: `javac` says `count has private access in Shelf`. What is the right first move?
hint: The class's author closed it on purpose.

choices.text: Change `count` to `public` in `Shelf`
choices.why: That removes the protection the class relied on; look for the intended way in first.

choices.text: Look for a public method that does what you need, such as `count()`
choices.why: Right: a private field is usually paired with methods that offer the safe operations.

choices.text: Move your class into `Shelf`'s package
choices.why: Package-mates are refused too; `Inside` was.

choices.text: Compile with `-g`, which relaxes access checks
choices.why: `-g` adds debugging names and changes no rule.

prompt: `Catalogue.java` holds `public class Catalogue` and a non-public `class Entry`. A class in another package writes `new Entry()`. What happens?
hint: Package-private applies to classes as well as to members.

choices.text: It works, because `Entry` sits in a public class's file
choices.why: Sharing a file shares nothing about access.

choices.text: A compile error: the class is invisible to that code
choices.why: Right: a non-public class is package-private, like a member with no modifier.

choices.text: It compiles, and fails at run time when `Entry.class` is not found
choices.why: The compiler refuses it first; it never reaches the JVM.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson's advice, start from private, lead you to? Choose all that apply.
hint: Open only what another class has a reason to use.

choices.text: Fields `private`, read through methods where others need the value
choices.why: Yes: like `count` and `count()`, `renewals` and `renewals()`.

choices.text: Every method `public`, so the class is easy to use
choices.why: Methods too are as closed as they can be; open each one when it has a caller outside.

choices.text: A helper method that only its own class calls stays `private`
choices.why: Yes: nobody outside needs it, so nobody outside gets it.

choices.text: Fields `protected`, in case a subclass needs them one day
choices.why: "In case" is not a reason; a subclass that needs one can be given a method then.

prompt: Which modifier did `Shelf` use for its method `add()`, so that `Main` in another package could call it?
hint: `Main` is outside `lib`.

choices.text: `public`
choices.why: Right: only public reaches a class in another package that is not a subclass.

choices.text: None, since methods are public unless marked otherwise
choices.why: With no modifier a method is package-private, like a field.

choices.text: `protected`, which includes callers in other packages
choices.why: Protected adds subclasses only, and `Main` is not one.
